motivo: Reportaje de reserva, sin mensajes de la semana, sobre un asunto de fondo que no caduca en un mes: a qué edad puede usar IA el alumnado. Es el hilo común de tres documentos de la Biblioteca digital que no han tenido reportaje (el informe para la UNESCO de Livingstone y otras autoras, el white paper del Foro Económico Mundial sobre infancia e IA y las Orientacions catalanas de 2026) y del debate que abrió en ChatGPT-IA-edu el anuncio de Google sobre la IA desactivada por defecto en cuentas escolares. Tiene actores (empresas con edades mínimas distintas, AEPD, INTEF, comunidades autónomas, UNESCO, WEF, UE), normativa (artículo 7 de la LOPDGDD, Reglamento europeo de IA, el proyecto de ley que elevaba la edad a 16 años y que ha caducado) y consecuencias prácticas para cualquier docente de primaria o ESO. El reportaje anterior (agentes de IA y datos del alumnado) solo rozó el tema. Las condiciones de las empresas, que cambian, van fechadas.
antetitulo: AI and age in the classroom
titular: The age for using AI in class depends on three different rules, and none is enough on its own
entradilla: Each service’s terms, data protection law and educational guidance set different ages for using artificial intelligence, and they are often confused. This report explains what each says as of 6 November 2026, why research asks us to swap the question of age for the question of purpose, and how a primary or secondary teacher can decide which tool to use, with which account, and who operates it.

parrafos: When a teacher wonders whether their students can use an artificial intelligence assistant, they usually look for a number. But at least three rules of different origin coexist. The first is the minimum age each company sets in its terms of use, a contract between the company and whoever opens the account. The second is the age from which a minor can consent by themselves to the processing of their data, which Spanish law sets at 14. The third is the recommendations of education authorities, which guide what is considered prudent in a classroom.

The three answer different questions and do not coincide. That a service admits accounts from the age of 13 does not mean it is suitable for a Year 8 class, or that a school can ask its students to sign up for it. And that a student has turned 14 does not settle whether the tool has an educational purpose. **What matters is not only the students’ age, but who opens the account, who operates the tool and what it is used for.**

As of 6 November 2026, [OpenAI’s terms of use for Europe](https://openai.com/policies/eu-terms-of-use/) require users to be at least 13 or the minimum age their country requires to consent, and ask for the permission of a parent or legal guardian for those under 18. Its [help centre](https://help.openai.com/es-es/articles/8313401-es-chatgpt-seguro-para-todas-las-edades) (in Spanish) adds a note aimed at the classroom: if ChatGPT is used for educational purposes with children under 13, the direct interaction with the tool must be carried out by an adult.

Google distinguishes two worlds. With a personal account, its help pages say that in Spain you need to be [at least 14 to manage your own Google Account](https://support.google.com/accounts/answer/1350409?hl=en); the Gemini apps ask for [13 or the age set by each country](https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/13278668?hl=en), but they are [not available for supervised accounts](https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/16109150?hl=en) with Family Link in the European Economic Area, and to use them with a [paid AI plan in the European Economic Area](https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/14517446?hl=en) you must be over 18. With a Google Workspace for Education account, by contrast, the [guide for schools](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/getting-started/editions/quickstart-guide-to-gemini-and-gemini-notebook-for-education?hl=es) (in Spanish), updated on 28 October 2026, presents Gemini and Gemini Notebook as available to all ages, with access managed by the administrator, more heavily filtered content for under-18s and data that is not used to train models.

On those accounts, according to the [age-based access control page](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/getting-started/editions/control-access-to-google-services-by-age?hl=es) (in Spanish), in primary and secondary schools anyone not identified by the administrator as over 18 gets a restricted experience: for example, they cannot use Gemini in Classroom to create or edit content. In addition, according to [Engadget](https://www.engadget.com/2305432/google-says-that-students-in-schools-that-ban-ai-wont-have-access-to-search/), Google announced that Gemini and search will be switched off by default in primary and secondary school accounts until the school turns them on, with a rollout “in the coming months”; the newspaper covered [the debate that announcement sparked about who decides in a school](pieza:2026-11-03/google-ia-cuentas-escolares).

Microsoft sets a minimum age of 13 in the [Copilot terms for individuals](https://www.microsoft.com/en-gb/microsoft-copilot/for-individuals/termsofuse), which apply from 18 August 2026, and which may be higher depending on each country’s law, and it warns that it may switch off or limit features for under-18s. For schools, its education blog announced in August 2025 [Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat for students aged 13 and over](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/blog/educationblog/microsoft-365-copilot-chat-for-students-13/4440370), managed by administrators and without using the data to train foundation models. Anthropic is the most restrictive: the [Claude consumer terms](https://www.anthropic.com/legal/consumer-terms), in force since 8 October 2025, require users to be at least 18.

apartados.ladillo: The law: fourteen, and the educational function
parrafos: [Article 7 of the Data Protection Act](https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2018-16673#a7) (in Spanish) establishes that the processing of a minor’s data can be based on their consent only when they are over fourteen; below that, it is lawful only with the consent of the holder of parental authority or guardianship, as the [Spanish Data Protection Agency](https://www.aepd.es/preguntas-frecuentes/10-menores-y-educacion/FAQ-1001-cual-es-la-edad-para-que-los-menores-puedan-prestar-consentimiento-para-tratar-sus-datos-personales) (in Spanish) reminds us. It is the age that counts when a student opens a commercial service on their own.

At school, however, consent is not the usual basis. The AEPD explains that in compulsory and regulated education [neither students’ nor families’ consent is needed](https://www.aepd.es/preguntas-frecuentes/10-menores-y-educacion/FAQ-1009-pueden-los-centros-educativos-impartir-clases-y-realizar-examenes-online-sin-el-consentimiento-de-los-interesados) (in Spanish) for processing linked to the educational function, because it answers a public-interest mission set out in the Education Act. The platforms are chosen by the school or the administration, with the advice of its data protection officer, and teachers must use the means these put at their disposal. The difference is clear: using a tool contracted by the education authority is not the same as asking a 12-year-old to register for a commercial service.

That age of 14 could have changed. The [Bill to protect minors in digital environments](https://www.congreso.es/public_oficiales/L15/CONG/BOCG/A/BOCG-15-A-52-1.PDF) (in Spanish), introduced in March 2025, included raising it to 16. According to its [page on the Congress website](https://www.congreso.es/es/proyectos-de-ley?p_p_id=iniciativas&p_p_lifecycle=0&p_p_state=normal&p_p_mode=view&_iniciativas_mode=mostrarDetalle&_iniciativas_legislatura=XV&_iniciativas_id=121%2F000052) (in Spanish), consulted on 6 November 2026, the initiative is listed as lapsed since 6 October 2026, the date the Cortes were dissolved. The age in force therefore remains 14.

The European framework adds two pieces. The [AI Act](https://www.boe.es/buscar/doc.php?id=DOUE-L-2024-81079) (in Spanish) prohibits systems that exploit vulnerabilities arising from age and classes as high-risk those used in education to decide access or assess outcomes. According to the [European Commission](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/regulatory-framework-ai), the AI literacy obligation has applied since 2 February 2025, and the high-risk obligations of Annex III have been postponed to 2 December 2027.

Catalonia has the most detailed criterion. Its *Orientacions per a l’ús de la intel·ligència artificial als centres educatius*, published by the Department of Education and Vocational Training in September 2026 ([the newspaper’s review in its Library](pieza:2026-11-02/cat-orientacions-ia)), state that students under 14 should not use general-purpose AI autonomously: if they work with it, the teacher operates it. Between 14 and 18 they recommend families’ authorisation even though the legal basis is the public-interest mission, and they place students’ direct interaction from the second term of Year 9 (3.º de ESO).

The [Basque Government’s guide to the use of AI in education](https://www.euskadi.eus/contenidos/documentacion/inn_doc_adi_artif/es_def/adjuntos/Guia-uso-de-IA-en-educacion_Euskadi.pdf) (in Spanish) states in its introduction that the age limit for using chatbots is 13, so that those younger cannot use them. The Canary Islands do not set ages, but their [recommendations of 13 January 2026](https://www3.gobiernodecanarias.org/medusa/ecoescuela/ia/2026/01/13/recomendacionesusoia/) (in Spanish) present, as AI tools in Google’s education environment, Gemini for teachers and NotebookLM for teachers and students. The guidance of the other regions could not be reviewed for this report.

At national level, INTEF’s [Guide to the use of artificial intelligence in education](https://intef.es/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/ACTUALIZACION-GUIA-DE-LA-IA-DEF-1-SEPT-2026-Publicable-v5-2.pdf) (in Spanish), version 2.0, [published on 8 September 2026](https://intef.es/Noticias/nueva-version-de-la-guia-sobre-el-uso-de-la-inteligencia-artificial-en-el-ambito-educativo/) (in Spanish), asks schools to prioritise tools authorised or validated by education authorities and to strengthen students’ AI literacy.

UNESCO put a figure on it in 2023: its guidance on generative AI in education [proposed a minimum age of 13](https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/unesco-governments-must-quickly-regulate-generative-ai-schools) for using these tools in the classroom. Three years later, a research report published by UNESCO itself, written by Sonia Livingstone, Kim R. Sylwander, Sandra El Gemayel and Ayça Atabey, argues that there is no right age, and the newspaper [covered it in its Library](pieza:2026-11-02/unesco-edad-ia). In her [summary on the Media@LSE blog](https://blogs.lse.ac.uk/medialse/2026/09/22/is-there-a-right-age-for-ai-in-education/), Livingstone explains that developmental science now sees variability and context as the norm, and that without attention to child development and clear educational purposes, ministries risk deciding without foundation.

The report also proposes distinguishing between educating students about AI, a literacy that should start early, and using AI to educate, where the evidence of benefits is scarce. That is why Livingstone considers the precautionary principle “a reasonable starting point”. She also cites Common Sense Media: 73% of American teenagers say they have never talked to a teacher about what AI is and how it works. The summary does not give the sample size.

The [World Economic Forum](https://reports.weforum.org/docs/WEF_Childrens_Safety_and_WellBeing_in_the_Age_of_AI_2026.pdf), in a white paper from September 2026, offers the view opposed to broad bans. It argues that age verification is useful for applying differentiated safeguards, but does not determine maturity or guarantee moderation or redress for harm, and that blanket restrictions can block benefits and push children towards less controlled services. The two positions share the substance: age alone does not make a tool safe or useful.

With students under 14, the most prudent option, and the one consistent with the guidance, is mediated use: the teacher operates the tool with their school account, projects and comments, and students analyse, check and discuss the answers without entering personal data. This way AI literacy can be taught from primary school, for example by checking a chatbot’s errors or comparing its answer with a book, without any child opening an account.

When students are going to use the tool directly, it is best to do so with the educational account provided by the administration and not a personal one, after checking that the school’s administrator has enabled it and with what limitations. **A personal account opened by a minor falls outside the school’s umbrella and depends on consent and the company’s terms.** If in doubt about a particular tool, the education authority’s data protection officer can advise.

Informing families about which tool is used, with which account and for what is good practice, even if the law does not always require their consent. Before each activity, the questions raised by the research help: what educational purpose does it serve, what evidence supports it, and is it about learning about AI or with it. And it is worth reviewing the services’ terms from time to time, because they change often.

claves: Three different ages coexist: the one in each service’s terms, the age of consent for data processing (14 in Spain) and the one educational guidance recommends.
As of 6 November 2026, OpenAI and Microsoft ask for at least 13, Anthropic 18, and Google opens Gemini to all ages only in educational accounts managed by the school.
In regulated education, data processing rests on the educational function, not on consent, as long as the tools provided by the school or the authority are used.
The bill that would have raised the age of consent to 16 lapsed when the Cortes were dissolved in October 2026.
UNESCO and the World Economic Forum agree that age alone is not enough: purpose, conditions and evidence matter.

ilustracion: Infografía en tres franjas horizontales, una por regla, sobre una regla graduada de 0 a 18 años. Franja 1, «Condiciones de las empresas»: marcas en 13 (OpenAI, Microsoft, Gemini personal), 18 (Anthropic) y un tramo sombreado «todas las edades, solo con cuenta del centro» para Gemini en Workspace for Education. Franja 2, «Ley de protección de datos»: una línea en 14 años, «consentimiento propio», con la nota «en el centro, la base es la función educativa». Franja 3, «Guías educativas»: Cataluña, menos de 14 «lo maneja el docente» y de 14 a 18 «con autorización»; Euskadi, sin chatbots antes de 13. Al pie, tres preguntas que sustituyen a «¿qué edad?»: ¿para qué?, ¿con qué cuenta?, ¿quién la maneja?
ilustracion_alt: Infographic on an age ruler from 0 to 18, with marks at 13, 14 and 18. First band, “Companies”: a band covering all ages, labelled “School”, for Gemini in educational accounts, and a line from age 13 (OpenAI, Microsoft) to 18 (Anthropic). Second band, “Data law”: a set of scales and a line that changes at 14, the age of own consent. Third band, “Guidance”: two lines, one with a step at 14 and another starting at 13, with a red cross before that age. At the bottom, the box “What for? With which account? Who operates it?”.
